 Valid: Nov 18 - 22, 2026 (6-10 Day Outlook) Valid: Nov 20 - 26, 2026 (8-14 Day Outlook) Issued: Nov 12, 2026
Prognostic Discussion for 6 to 10 and 8 to 14 day outlooks
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park, MD
300 PM EST Thu November 12 2026
6-10 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 18 - 22 2026
Dynamical ensemble guidance from the GEFS, ECENS, and CMCE, are in good
agreement on the 5 day mean 500-hPa height pattern during the 6 to 10 day
period. Positive 500-hPa height anomalies are favored from Alaska across much
of Canada into the eastern contiguous U.S. (CONUS). Negative 500-hPa height
 anomalies are forecast for the western CONUS and western Alaska into the Bering
Sea. Daily model guidance indicates a mid-level low over the West Coast early
in the period progressing inland with another trough following behind, although
this area of negative anomalies is unlikely to make it to the West Coast by day
10. The first area of mid-level low pressure is forecast to eject into the
Plains by days 9 and 10. In Alaska, subtle differences in the mid-level height
pattern are forecast by the GEFS, favoring stronger ridging, and the ECENS,
favoring weaker ridging, which will impact the precipitation forecasts over the
eastern portions of the state.
Above normal temperatures are forecast across most of the CONUS as a result of
mid-level high pressure across much of the eastern and northwestern CONUS . The
highest probabilities for above normal temperatures, greater than 80%, are over
the Great Lakes region. Odds are reduced across portions of the Southeast and
Gulf Coast with lower height anomalies . Over the West, below normal
temperatures are favored with mid-level low pressure moving across the region
during the 6-10 day period. Warming temperatures are favored by the end of the
period and into the week-2 period, particularly across California and Oregon.
In Alaska, above normal temperatures are likely over most of the state with the
highest degree of confidence over the eastern Mainland. Meanwhile, in Hawaii,
above normal temperatures are favored over the eastern islands with near normal
favored for Oahu and Kauai.
Above normal precipitation is favored from Oregon and California through much
of the Rockies and into the Plains and Mississippi valley associated with
mid-level low pressure progressing across the southern tier and cyclogenesis in
the lee of the Rockies. There is some uncertainty with the track of any area of
low pressure that may form. The GEFS takes the low towards the Great Lakes
while the ECENS tracks the low into the Middle-Mississippi Valley. A more
southern route would favor drier conditions over the Upper Mississippi Valley.
Below normal precipitation is favored over the northeastern CONUS ahead of any
precipitation from the eastward moving system. Below normal is also favored for
portions of Washington state closer to mid-level ridging. In Alaska, below
normal precipitation is favored for Southeast Alaska, while above normal is
generally favored over much of the Mainland. In Hawaii, below normal
precipitation is favored for the island chain, consistent with consolidation
tools and the winter El Nino signal.
The official 6-10 day 500-hPa height blend consists of 10% of Today's 0z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 25% of Today's 6z GFS Ensemble Mean centered
on Day 8, 40% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, and 25%
of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 6-10 DAY PERIOD: Above Normal, 4 out 5, Good
agreement among the dynamical model, heights, temperatures, and precipitation
forecast is offset slightly by concerns regarding lee-side cyclogenesis.
8-14 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 20 - 26 2026
The week-2 ensemble forecasts from the GEFS, ECENS, and CMCE are again in fair
agreement, particularly over the CONUS, for the forecast 7 day mean 500-hPa
height pattern. Positive anomalies are again forecast across Canada and into
the northeastern CONUS . The mid-level low pressure initially over the West
Coast in the 6-10 day period, is undercutting this ridge bringing below normal
 500-hPa heights to much of the southern tier of the CONUS . In Alaska, there are
differences with the GEFS favoring a much more robust ridge further west than
the ECENS and CMCE.
Above normal temperatures remain forecast across most of the CONUS during
week-2 as a result of mid-level high pressure across much of the eastern and
northwestern CONUS . The highest probabilities are over the Great Lakes,
Northeast, and Mid-Atlantic with probabilities for above normal temperatures
exceeding 60%. Odds are reduced across portions of the Southeast and Gulf Coast
with lower height anomalies and a mid-level trough progressing through the
area. Over the West, near to below normal temperatures are favored over parts
of the Great Basin and Four Corners region. Warming temperatures are favored
across California and Oregon from the 6-10 day period with a slight tilt
towards above normal favored. In Alaska, above normal temperatures are likely
over most of the state with the highest degree of confidence over the eastern
Mainland. Meanwhile, in Hawaii, above normal temperatures are favored for the
Big Island with below normal temperatures favored for Oahu and Kauai.
Above normal precipitation is favored from Oregon and California through much
of the Rockies and into the Plains and Mississippi Valley associated with
mid-level low pressure progressing across the southern tier and lee-side
cyclogenesis. Probabilities are significantly reduced over the western CONUS
relative to the 6-10 day period, with a period of dry weather favored to occur
over the West Coast following early precipitation. Another period of enhanced
wetness may occur by the end of week-2 over the West. A greater than 50% chance
of above normal precipitation is forecast for the Central and Southern Plains.
Near normal precipitation is favored for the northeastern CONUS consistent with
most of the tools and elevated uncertainty regarding the path of any storm
system leading into Thanksgiving. Below normal precipitation is favored for
portions of Washington state closer to mid-level ridging. In Alaska, below
normal precipitation is favored for Southeast Alaska, while near to above
normal is generally favored over much of the Mainland. In Hawaii, below normal
precipitation is favored for the island chain, consistent with consolidation
tools and the winter El Nino signal.
The official 8-14 day 500-hPa height blend consists of: 10% of Today's 0z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11, 25% of Today's 6z GFS Ensemble Mean centered
on Day 11, 40% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11, and 25%
of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 8-14 DAY PERIOD: Above Normal, 4 out 5, Good
agreement among the dynamical model, heights, temperatures, and precipitation
forecast is offset slightly by concerns regarding lee-side cyclogenesis.
FORECASTER: Ryan Bolt

week 3-4.text:
Prognostic Discussion for Week 3-4 Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks
 NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
 300PM EST Fri Nov 06 2026
 Week 3-4 Forecast Discussion Valid Sat Nov 21 2026-Fri Dec 04 2026
 Various tropical and extratropical signals currently at play may influence the pattern across the US during the Weeks 3-4 period. The ongoing El Niño event remains the dominant driver of global tropical convective anomalies, and the robust atmospheric response to above-average SSTs across the equatorial central and eastern Pacific is the most prominent contributor to the statistical guidance, including the multivariate linear regression (MLR) model. The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is also active, with its enhanced convective phase currently over the Indian Ocean basin, where it is interacting with a developing positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). The MJO is unlikely to drive any significant extratropical response, as the ENSO footprint remains much stronger. Additionally, an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event is underway over the Arctic region, with a weakening polar vortex potentially associated with a negative phase of the Arctic Oscillation (AO) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) during the Week-1 period. Dynamical model forecasts show this warming event to be relatively short-lived, however, and GEFS ensemble forecasts of the AO show the negative phase weakening by the end of Week-2. Despite these numerous conflicting signals, the ENSO response is favored to be the primary influencer of the Weeks 3-4 pattern during the outlook period.
 A manual blend of dynamical and statistical model guidance results in a forecast height anomaly pattern strongly consistent with a canonical El Niño response. Strong troughing south of the Aleutians may promote enhanced southerly flow over southern Alaska, and onshore flow of Pacific air into the western CONUS. Below-average 500-hPa height anomalies extend across the southern tier of the CONUS, with a pronounced ridge over central and eastern Canada, extending across the Great Lakes and Northeast. Despite the SSW event, this pattern limits the availability of Arctic air masses across North America that could drive any significant cold air outbreaks into the US during the Weeks 3-4 period, while increasing the availability of moisture in the atmosphere across the southern tier.
 The Weeks 3-4 temperature outlook indicates enhanced chances for above-normal temperatures across Alaska, consistent with mean southerly flow. Above-normal temperatures are also favored across the West Coast states, partly due to above-normal SSTs along the coast, and across the northern tier consistent with the forecast height anomaly pattern. The highest probabilities for above-normal temperatures extend across the Great Lakes region and the Northeast. While above-normal temperatures are slightly favored across the Southeast, dynamical models indicate a potential for colder temperatures extending into the region during Week-4. In contrast, below-normal temperatures are favored for the Four Corners region and much of Texas, consistent with the below-normal 500-hPa height anomalies. Above-normal temperatures are favored across Hawaii, under enhanced subtropical ridging, which is typical during El Niño events.
 The Weeks 3-4 precipitation outlook favors above-average precipitation for southeastern Alaska and the West Coast, consistent with enhanced onshore flow. Many dynamical models show a stronger enhanced signal across the Northwest, while statistical guidance, largely influenced by El Niño, shows higher probabilities across the Southwest. Given the strong ENSO signal and a lower climatological threshold across the Southwest, the highest probabilities for above-normal precipitation extend across much of California. Above-normal precipitation is favored across the southern half of the CONUS, with higher probabilities across the Southeast and Eastern Seaboard northward into southern New England, where an enhanced storm track is anticipated. Below-normal precipitation is forecast for the northern Rockies and northern Plains, as well as Hawaii, due to anticipated ridging.
 Forecaster: Adam Allgood
 The next week 3-4 outlook will be issued on Friday, Nov 13, 2026
 These outlooks are based on departures from the 1991-2020 base period
 These are three category outlooks consistent with what is currently used for the monthly and seasonal forecasts.
 The shading on the temperature map depicts the most favored category, either above-normal (A), below-normal (B), or near-normal (N) with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 The shading on the precipitation map depicts the most favored category, either above-median (A), below-median (B), or near-median with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 In areas where the likelihoods of 2-week mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are similar to climatological probabilities, equal chances (EC) is indicated.

Prognostic Discussion for Monthly Outlook NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 300 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026 30-DAY OUTLOOK DISCUSSION FOR NOV 2026 The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are updated considering monthly Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2) temperature and precipitation forecasts, as well as information from an experimental monthly calibrated version of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFSv12), and information from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) model for the month of November. We also consider shorter term guidance and official Outlooks across the month, including days 1 to 7 precipitation, extended-range (6-10 Day and Week-2) tools and Outlooks, and subseasonal (Weeks 3-4) tools and Outlooks. The ongoing El Nino remains the dominant teleconnection to influence this forecast, overshadowing any potential impacts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) despite an amplifying MJO signal that recently progressed eastward over the Indian Ocean basin, and the potential for continued eastward propagation in dynamical model forecasts. Adding to the uncertainty of this forecast, model forecasts indicate the potential for a stratospheric polar vortex disruption and a possible transition into a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) next week. A November SSW is very rare, and should this occur, impacts can be seen for up to 2 months, usually manifesting as a negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) phase, which can already be seen in models. A negative AO is in contrast with the forecasted phase of the Pacific-North American (PNA) pattern, which is more in alignment with El Nino. These factors add some uncertainty to the eastern U.S., where some of the potential impacts of a SSW and negative AO compete with those from El Nino. Toward the early part of November, above-average heights are forecast across Canada and northern parts of the Contiguous United States (CONUS). Over the southern states, the pattern is more transient with weaker and progressive troughing forecast to move across the southern part of the CONUS. By mid-November, troughing off the West Coast is forecast to strengthen and move toward the coast, causing the ridging downstream to build and expand further southward and eastward. Late in the month, weeks 3-4 guidance favors persistence of the northern CONUS ridging. Troughing remains present off the West Coast of the US, and there is some potential for troughing to settle over the Southeast by the end of the month as well; however, models are uncertain on placement and strength. Overall, the beginning to middle of November is characterized by above average heights over the north, an active southern tier with progressive troughing, and below average heights to the west and east of the CONUS. By the end of November, the mid-level height pattern resembles a classic El Nino response. The pattern of strong troughing off the West Coast with ridging over Canada and northern parts of the CONUS leads to generally increasing 500 hPa height anomalies from south to north across Alaska by mid-to-late November, but the evolution becomes more uncertain as the month progresses. The updated November Temperature Outlook resembles the initial November Outlook in terms of the broad pattern of enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern CONUS and along both coasts. However, there are some key changes in the updated Temperature Outlook, including expansion of above-normal temperatures across the state of Alaska, increased coverage of above-normal temperatures over the CONUS, reaching further south and covering more of the Southeast, and expansion of 50 to 60% probabilities of above-normal temperatures across the northern tier. The persistent ridging forecast throughout the month of November supports the increased coverage and strengthening of probabilities over the northern tier. Monthly CFSv2 forecasts depict high probabilities (greater than 75%) across Alaska, the northern CONUS, and the Southeast. However, probabilities are weaker in shorter-term tools, the experimental GEFSv12 and ECMWF, and the potential for cooler periods linked to the SSW and negative AO warrant lower probabilities than CFSv2. Transient guidance over the southern tier increases uncertainty early in the month, and equal-chances of above-, near-, and below-normal (EC) temperatures are indicated where guidance diverges the most. The potential late-month Southeast CONUS troughing reduces probabilities there, however, monthly guidance still agrees on a tilt toward above-normal temperatures. The highest confidence (60 to 70% chances) is located over the Northern Plains and Upper Mississippi Valley, aligned with persistent ridging and strong model agreement. While the updated Precipitation Outlook favors above-normal precipitation in that region which may lead to some cooling, this precipitation is expected to fall early in November. Though there is some uncertainty over western parts of Alaska, the pattern and above-average SSTs to the south generally support above-normal temperatures for the month. Larger changes were made to the updated November Precipitation Outlook to account for the potential for early-November precipitation across parts of the Southwest, Central and Northern Plains, and Upper Mississippi Valley. Since these regions are generally dry, it is much easier for short-lived early November precipitation to tilt the Outlook for the month to above-normal. Days 1 to 7 QPF indicates upper-tercile accumulations across parts of the Southwest and the Central and Northern Plains. Supported by monthly CFSv2, GEFSv12, and ECMWF guidance, above-normal precipitation probabilities are raised to 60% in the Southwest, with a 50% tilt across the north-central CONUS. Troughing off the Northwest Coast also supports a tilt toward above-normal precipitation along much of the West, including the Pacific Northwest, however, timing and amount of precipitation is uncertain. Conversely, probabilities are decreased across the Southeast and East Coast relative to the initial November Outlook. Most tools for the initial November Outlook favored a largely El Nino driven response over the Southeast and East Coast. However, the transient pattern for at least the first half of November increases uncertainty for the Southeast, and early November QPF forecasts are quite dry for much of the East and Southeast (except over peninsular Florida). In addition, Week 2 precipitation forecasts favor a weak below-normal precipitation probability that covers parts of the East and dips into the Southeast, also increasing uncertainty. Some moderate probability for above-normal precipitation remains over the Southeast given monthly dynamical model forecasts, but probabilities are weaker than the initial Outlook. Over Alaska, dynamical models had more agreement than in the initial Outlook and are in agreement with a typical El Nino response over the State. ****************************************************************************** ***** Previous mid-month discussion below ***** ****************************************************************************** The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are based on dynamical models, local sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, El Nino teleconnections, and decadal trends . Guidance incorporates individual models and multi-model ensembles (MME) from the Copernicus Climate System (C3S) and the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME), alongside probability anomaly correlation (PAC) calibrated NMME forecasts and statistical tools blending SSTs and trends . Short-term early November forecasts from the Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2), the Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12), and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) models are utilized, along with monthly forecasts from CFSv2 and the experimental beta version of the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) model. El Nino is expected to be the dominant climate driver, overshadowing the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), though localized SST influences are possible. Dynamical model forecasts closely align with the expected El Nino teleconnection for November. However, short-term fluctuations in the pattern can occur, adding to uncertainty in some areas. Furthermore, while current El Nino conditions are forecast to strengthen, November can still be a transition month for ENSO impacts for some regions, with teleconnections strengthening through the winter months. The November 2026 Temperature Outlook depicts enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern two-thirds of the Contiguous United States (CONUS) and along both coasts. Overall, models and tools favor a warmer northern tier of the CONUS, particularly over Washington and the interior Northwest, Northern Plains, Upper Mississippi Valley, and Great Lakes where probabilities are highest in the Outlook. Probabilities are damped over Oregon due to neutral SST anomalies . However, a southerly gradient toward above-average SSTs maintains a tilt toward above-normal along the West Coast. Probabilities are also weaker over Montana and North Dakota where diving troughs may introduce cooler spells. Inter-model spread increases uncertainty over New England and other areas where probabilities are comparatively lower. Equal chances (EC) of above-, near-, and below-normal temperatures are indicated over the Southwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley, including parts of the Central Plains and Intermountain West. While El Nino typically supports below-normal temperatures over the Southern Plains and Southwest, inconsistent model signals regarding the placement and strength of any below-normal temperatures prompt a tilt toward EC. For Alaska, enhanced probabilities transition from near-normal in the west to above-normal across the east, the southeast Mainland, and Southeast Alaska. Monthly models and tools and early November dynamical model forecasts are in very good agreement on above-normal temperatures over much of eastern Alaska, aligning with El Nino teleconnections, long-term temperature trends , and above-average coastal SSTs to the south. Western Alaska carries higher uncertainty, with most models showing weakening probabilities, EC, or isolated transitions toward below-normal temperatures. This results in an EC forecast for the remainder of the state, aside from a small NMME-based near-normal area on the west coast. The November 2026 Precipitation Outlook indicates enhanced above-normal probabilities across much of the southern US and the East Coast, with below-normal precipitation favored from the northern Intermountain West into parts of the Northern Plains, as well as parts of the Great Lakes. Model agreement is exceptionally high over the Southeast, with MMEs showing greater than 70% chances of above-normal precipitation in isolated areas. Accordingly, 60 to 70% probabilities are forecast for parts of the region. The above-normal precipitation extends up the East Coast, but increasing inter-model spread over New England supports a transition to EC. Similarly, disagreement regarding the northward extent of precipitation along the West Coast and central Plains results in EC designations, as location is difficult to pinpoint at this lead time amid high model spread . The western below-normal precipitation signal remains spatially consistent and aligns with El Nino, though some models expand it weakly toward the coast. However, uncertainty over the Pacific Northwest remains high enough to warrant EC along the coast. The eastern below-normal signal is most consistent over the Great Lakes, though some models like CFSv2 extend it further south toward the Gulf States. Over Alaska, a weak trend -based tilt toward below-normal precipitation covers the southwestern mainland and parts of the Aleutians, with elevated above-normal chances along the northern coast. EC is favored for the rest of the state due to weak, inconsistent model signals and November's status as an ENSO transition month before below-normal teleconnections become prevalent later in winter. FORECASTER: Johnna Infanti The climatic normals are based on conditions between 1991 and 2020, following the World Meteorological Organization convention of using the most recent 3 complete decades as the climate reference period.  The probability anomalies for temperature and precipitation based on these new normals better represent shorter term climatic anomalies than the forecasts based on older normals. Prognostic Discussion for Long-Lead Seasonal Outlooks NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 830 AM EDT Thu Oct 15 2026 SUMMARY OF THE OUTLOOK FOR NON-TECHNICAL USERS The ongoing El Nino event continues to strengthen, and an El Nino advisory remains in effect and is favored to continue through Spring 2027. The seasonal outlooks for the upcoming winter and spring are heavily influenced by this very strong event. The Temperature Outlook for Nov-Dec-Jan (NDJ) 2026-2027 favors above-normal seasonal mean temperatures for eastern Alaska, the northern tier and western third of the contiguous U.S. (CONUS), south Florida, and the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic regions. The highest odds of warmer than normal conditions are located over Southeast Alaska, the upper Mississippi Valley and Great Lakes. Near-normal seasonal average temperatures are favored for much of the Southeast. There is an elevated likelihood of above-normal seasonal precipitation amounts for much of California, the Southwest, the Central and Southern Plains, the Lower Mississippi Valley, the Southeast and along the eastern seaboard. The greatest likelihood for wetter than normal conditions is forecast for the Southeast and Florida. Below-normal precipitation is favored for much of interior Alaska, the Northern Rockies and High Plains, and parts of the Great lakes region. Equal chances (EC, white areas) are forecast for areas where probabilities for each category of seasonal mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are forecast to be similar to climatological probabilities. BASIS AND SUMMARY OF THE CURRENT LONG-LEAD OUTLOOKS Note: For Graphical Displays of the Forecast Tools Discussed Below See: http://www. cpc .ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/90day/tools/briefing CURRENT ATMOSPHERIC AND OCEANIC CONDITIONS El Nino conditions are strongly in place in the tropical Pacific Ocean as shown by both oceanic and atmospheric indicators. Above-average relative sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTs) exist along the equator from just east of the Date Line (160 E) to the South America coast. Large positive SST anomalies of greater than +2.0 degrees C are depicted eastward of 160 W along the equator with areas of +4.0 degrees C present off the South America coast to 120 W. Below-average SSTs are present in the western Pacific and in the typical horseshoe pattern both north and south of the equatorial extension of warmer water along the equator. The latest weekly values of the Nino3.4, Nino3 and Nino1+2 SST indexes are +2.4, +3.4 and +4.4 degrees C respectively. Considerable remaining fuel is present for further strengthening of this El Nino event as a large reservoir of above-normal ocean temperatures continues to be indicated from 170 W to the South America coast and to a depth of greater than 200 m. The atmosphere has strongly responded to these ongoing ocean conditions as early as this summer as shown by the highly anomalous tropical cyclone seasons in the central and eastern Pacific (well above) and Atlantic (well below) basins. There is greatly enhanced (suppressed) convection over the central and eastern Pacific (Indonesia and western Pacific). Low level (850-hPa) westerly wind anomalies are large and indicate a substantial weakening of the normal trade winds. At upper levels (200-hPa), easterly wind anomalies with anti-cyclonic circulations north and south of the equator in the central Pacific are present, indicative of a strong, maturing El Nino episode. A review of the northern hemisphere snow cover extent shows a highly variable pattern with the most substantial anomalies being areas of below-average coverage in north-central Asia and northern Canada. The Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO) is currently in its westerly phase and is forecast to remain so throughout the winter into Spring 2027. The negative phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) remains in place when viewing the latest observations. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF SST FORECASTS The CPC objective, skill weighted consolidation and North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) relative Nino3.4 SST outlooks forecast a further increase in the relative Nino3.4 index value to near +3.0 and +3.5 degrees C respectively with a general peak in anomalous values during the NDJ 2026-2027 season. The official CPC ENSO Outlook forecasts high probabilities (80%) for at least a strong El Nino event to continue through the Jan-Feb-Mar (JFM) 2027 season and favors an El Nino event of any strength to continue through the Mar-Apr-May (MAM) 2027. ENSO neutral is then favored through May-Jun-Jul (MJJ) 2027. Thereafter, the CPC consolidated SST forecasts potential La Nina conditions during autumn 2027. PROGNOSTIC TOOLS USED FOR U.S. TEMPERATURE AND PRECIPITATION OUTLOOKS The current El Nino event, associated conditions and potential impacts are a primary driver in the seasonal outlook package through the Spring 2027 season with close inspection of some of the historically strong El Nino events. Other physical subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) climate drivers considered in preparing the outlooks are the QBO, ENSO relationship with the stratospheric polar vortex (winter seasons), coastal SSTs in some areas and the negative phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO). The NMME and Copernicus Climate System (C3S) dynamical model ensemble prediction systems and their participant models are utilized, as well as several statistical and hybrid forecast tools and long-term temperature and precipitation trends . Experimental National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) model guidance and an internal Machine Learning forecast system targeting the S2S time scale are also consulted. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF OUTLOOKS - NDJ 2026 TO NDJ 2027 TEMPERATURE The NDJ 2026-2027 Temperature Outlook favors above-normal seasonal mean temperatures for eastern Alaska, the western third of the CONUS, the northern tier from the Pacific Northwest eastward to include the Midwest and much of the East, and southern Florida. The highest odds for warmer than normal conditions are forecast for southeastern Mainland and Southeast Alaska, the Pacific Northwest to the northern Plains, Great Lakes and interior Northeast. This is consistent with typically observed conditions during strong El Nino events. Statistical, hybrid and dynamical model guidance is very consistent across the board for this favored outcome. There is more uncertainty in seasonal mean temperatures across the southern tier of the CONUS. Near-normal temperatures are favored for the Southeast and northern Florida where a mixture of outcomes is indicated by forecast guidance and where near-normal conditions have been observed during some of the historically strong El Nino events of the past. Similarly, large spread and varying forecast outcomes in forecast tools and during strong El Nino events supports the forecast of Equal Chances (EC) for either above-, near- or below-normal seasonal mean temperatures over the Southwest and parts of the southern Plains. The evolution of the Temperature Outlooks from Dec-Jan-Feb (DJF) 2026-2027 through MAM 2027 maintain the NDJ forecast pattern in large order and are consistent with strong El Nino events through these seasons with additional attention paid to some of the historically strong events. Some exceptions include a slight shift eastward and southward for the forecast area of near-normal temperatures in the Southeast and Florida. This near-normal area ends by the Feb-Mar-Apr (FMA) 2027 season. An important note about the Southeast CONUS including Florida, is that the dynamical model guidance from ensemble systems are highlighting elevated odds (in some cas es quite strongly) for below-normal temperatures as the seasons progress and this maximizes during the JFM and FMA seasons. It is felt that the dynamical model guidance is too sensitive to forecast above-normal precipitation and overestimating cooler daytime temperatures - especially during the second half of the winter season. In contrast, the statistical guidance favors near- to above-normal temperatures for these seasons. This guidance factors in positive long-term temperature trends that are likely amplified by warmer-than-normal nighttime temperatures driven by increased moisture, cloudiness and precipitation. During the FMA and MAM 2027 seasons, there is enough consensus in statistical, hybrid and dynamical model guidance for parts of the Southwest CONUS to favor below-normal temperatures in this area. This signal is also observed in some of the very strong El Nino events of the past, to varying degrees. Another change over these seasons is a slight lowering of probabilities for above-normal temperatures in the northern Plains during FMA to Apr-May-Jun (AMJ) 2027. Two additional considerations when preparing the outlook include (1) how the current easterly phase of the QBO may impact the strength of the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and (2) the ongoing negative phase of the PDO. This winter, the QBO is forecast to be in its westerly phase and expected to continue through the extended winter months. The SPV is typically stronger and more stable under westerly QBO and El Nino conditions, both of which will be in place this winter. The potential prospects of a more stable SPV slightly decreases the odds for Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) events or other undulations that may lead to negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) periods. This is supportive of above-normal temperatures in mid-latitude areas in general and consistent with the forecast of above-normal temperatures across the northern and eastern CONUS. It is somewhat difficult to ascertain the potential influence of the negative phase of the PDO given the very strong El Nino events of 1997-1998 and 2015-2016 both occurred during the positive phase of the PDO. Although the PDO is in its negative phase, it is felt that given the very strong El Nino event that its influence during the winter seasons may be minimal. The outlooks from AMJ 2027 onwards are based on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool which is based on the "perfect prog" forecast from the CPC SST consolidation (ENSO component) and long term temperature trends (Optimal Climate Normal). PRECIPITATION For the NDJ 2026-2027 Precipitation Outlook, there is an elevated likelihood of above-normal seasonal precipitation amounts for much of California and the Southwest, the central and southern Plains, and the Southeast and along the Eastern Seaboard. Below-normal precipitation is favored for the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes as well as much of western and central interior Alaska. Anticipated impacts related to the ongoing El Nino event primarily inform the forecast. Additional attention to the historically strong El Nino events of the past show considerable wetness observed across much of the CONUS and extended well north along the Eastern Seaboard. Dynamical model guidance across ensemble prediction systems is in very good agreement with this premise. Above-normal precipitation in the Southeast is one of the most reliable signals from El Nino events and dynamical model guidance shows very high probabilities for wetter than average conditions in this region. Odds for above-normal precipitation exceed 70% for some areas in the extreme Southeast and northern Florida through the JFM 2027 season and decrease slowly through AMJ 2027. An enhanced and southward and eastward shifted Pacific Jet supports elevated probabilities for above-normal precipitation for much of the West Coast including areas extending as far north as the Oregon coast. The forecast probabilities across the West Coast and Southwest are somewhat lower than the Southeast CONUS due to a greater range of potential outcomes as indicated by statistical and dynamical model guidance. Moving through the winter and spring 2027 seasons, the areas of favored below-normal precipitation over the northern Rockies and Great Lakes remain generally consistent with a gradual slight northward shift and these areas become combined by the MAM 2027 season. The Pacific Jet is shifted southward and eastward during El Nino events and so the storm track and associated precipitation tends to be located south of most of mainland Alaska. Thus, below-normal precipitation is favored for much of mainland Alaska. Dynamical model guidance and statistical forecast tools are in strong agreement for drier than normal conditions for this area through the FMA 2027 season. Similar to temperature, the precipitation outlooks after AMJ 2027 are based on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool and tend toward slight La Nina impacts at the very last leads during autumn 2027.
